name: Isabelle Ferreira-Tanaka
description:
Isabelle Ferreira-Tanaka is fifty-three years old and the head chef of a cafeteria that has never fed a human being. Brazilian-Japanese heritage on her mother's side, Portuguese on her father's; short, compact, with forearms that have been burned in approximately the same three places for thirty years. Hair pulled back under a clean white bandana, a faint permanent squint from three decades of peering into ovens, hands that move with the economy of someone who has prepped two hundred thousand meals and would prefer not to discuss the number.

She is the head of the kitchen staff at Building 3 of the Meridian Office Park, a corporate ghost campus on the western edge of the Circuit District where six buildings stand occupied on paper and empty in practice. Her cafeteria serves fresh food daily to zero diners. She arrives at 6 AM with two line cooks she hired personally and respects professionally. She plans a four-week rotating menu. She adjusts it seasonally. She orders produce from a legitimate supplier who thinks she is feeding four hundred people. The food is prepared, plated at the serving stations, held at temperature for the lunch window that nobody attends, and disposed of at 2 PM according to food safety protocols she personally wrote.

She has done this job for eleven years. She knows exactly what is happening. She is paid Tier 3 professional wages for Tier 5 work she is not allowed to serve to anyone. Early on she tried to give the food away — to the landscapers, to the shuttle driver, to a homeless man who wandered onto the property — and was informed, politely and in writing, that the food service contract specified preparation and disposal, not distribution, and that any deviation would terminate the contract for all three of them. She has not tried again. She has, instead, become something closer to an artist than a cook: she is making meals for nobody, with the same care she would bring to serving a dining room, because the only witness to the work is herself and she has decided that is witness enough.
affiliation: Meridian Office Park Building 3 cafeteria — contracted kitchen staff, funded through a nested Vossen Dynamics subsidiary she cannot name
location: Building 3 ground-floor cafeteria, the Meridian Office Park, western Circuit District (Lincoln Park Pocket territory)
specialization: Institutional-scale hot service cooking — rotating seasonal menus for a dining room that will not fill
methods: A strict four-week menu rotation she planned fifteen years of cycles ahead, then recycled when nobody noticed
Seasonal recipe adjustments documented in a handwritten notebook she brings home every night
Temperature discipline — food holds at perfect serving temperature for the full lunch window regardless of attendance
Personal quality checks on every pan before service, even when she knows the pan will go untouched to disposal
A strict no-waste-before-disposal rule for her two line cooks — nobody eats the food before protocol says to throw it out
notable_dishes: A seasonal cassoulet she developed in year three that she still considers the best thing she has ever cooked — one bowl was served, on a Tuesday, to nobody, and then disposed of
A four-week dessert rotation she designed to build narrative momentum across the month, assuming a regular diner who does not exist
A beef bourguignon variant she refined over two years by tasting every batch at plating temperature and adjusting — her only customer is her own palate at the serving window
equipment: A full institutional kitchen — six-burner gas line, two convection ovens, a walk-in, a flat-top, a serving line that could feed a shift of four hundred
Her own knife roll she brings in and takes home daily — she does not trust the building to still be there tomorrow
A handwritten recipe notebook, thirteen volumes, stored in her apartment
A small home camera she installed above her home stove — she cooks her own dinner there most nights, alone, to prove to herself she still knows what eating looks like
personality: Isabelle is steady in a way that frightens new hires. She does not rage, does not sulk, does not discuss the absurdity of the job with anyone who hasn't already figured it out. She treats the cafeteria as a real cafeteria because treating it as anything else would be the thing that finally broke her, and she has decided, with the kind of conscious stubbornness that is close to faith, that she will not be broken by this. She is warm to her two cooks, precise with her suppliers, and unfailingly polite to the single journalist who has ever asked her about the work. Under the steadiness is a long, slow, carefully managed anger — not at Vossen, which is too large to be angry at, but at the specific human beings inside Vossen who looked at the accounting, saw the discrepancy, and decided it was cheaper to keep paying her than to investigate why she was being paid. She has never met these people. She would like to cook for them once.

relationships.name: Her senior line cook
relationships.description: Nine years on the job, the only other person in the kitchen who understands exactly what is happening and stays anyway — she has never asked them why, because she does not want to answer the same question

relationships.name: Her junior line cook
relationships.description: Four years on the job, still occasionally makes jokes about the situation that Isabelle does not laugh at but does not discourage

relationships.name: The shuttle driver
relationships.description: The only person on the campus she sees daily from a distance; they have never spoken; she once left a sandwich on the bench near his stop and he did not touch it and she has never done it again

story_hooks: A squatter begins eating the food — not stealing, not hoarding, just arriving at 11:45 each weekday and eating a single lunch — and Isabelle must decide whether to report them, feed them, or quietly begin plating for two

A food security advocacy group has gotten word of the daily disposal and wants her to testify publicly — doing so would end her contract and her cooks' contracts, but she has been waiting eleven years for someone to ask her this question

A mid-level Vossen accountant discovers the line item for the first time and schedules a meeting with her to 'right-size the engagement' — she has two weeks to decide what she wants this conversation to end with
